title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Death and Resurrection: The Fog of Identity Opens

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a deep dive into one of the strangest, richest, most underrated novels in the English language.
Our Mutual Friend was Charles Dickens's last completed novel, and it is, in almost every sense, his most modern.
It opens on the Thames at night, with a man fishing — not for fish, but for corpses.
And from that extraordinary opening image, the novel spirals outward into wealth, dust, disguise, and the question of who we really are when stripped of name and money.
To explore all of this, I'm joined by three extraordinary readers of literature.

Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who is obsessed with how great fiction is actually built — the architecture of sentences, the single image that carries a chapter's weight.
She has a gift for making technical craft feel genuinely thrilling.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who brings the real world crashing into the fictional one — the actual institutions, the law, what poverty truly meant.
He can get genuinely angry about injustice, which, in a Dickens novel, is a considerable asset.
And Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels on audio than perhaps anyone alive.
He comes to every book as a performer first — hearing the rhythms, catching the comic timing, and knowing exactly when silence is the most eloquent choice.
We begin where the novel begins: on the river, in the dark, with a man and his daughter, and something terrible coming up from the water.
What Dickens does in that opening scene is something I find almost audacious in its compression.
We don't need to be told what Gaffer Hexam does for a living, or what kind of man he is.
Dickens gives us one gesture, and it tells us everything.
Gaffer pulls himself back into the boat, washes his arms over the side — and then washes what he's holding too.
"He chinked it once, and he blew upon it once, and he spat upon it once,—'for luck,' he hoarsely said—before he put it in his pocket."
That triple rhythm — chinked, blew, spat — is pure incantation.
It's the ritual of a man who has made a religion out of dead men's money, and Dickens captures it in a single sentence.
What gets me — and I've read that passage aloud more than once — is the word 'hoarsely.'
He doesn't just say 'for luck.' He says it hoarsely.
There's something caught in his throat — guilt, river damp, superstition — Dickens doesn't specify, and he doesn't need to.
When you perform that line, you have to decide where the voice comes from, and whichever choice you make, it's troubling.
That's the genius of it — the text is indeterminate in the best possible way.
It's worth being precise about what Gaffer is actually doing, because Victorian readers would have understood it immediately and we tend to soften it.
He is a mudlark — or more precisely, a body-finder — someone who searched the Thames for the drowned and was legally entitled to whatever was found on the corpse.
This was an actual, recognized occupation in nineteenth-century London.
The Thames was, among other things, an economy of the dead.
So that coin Gaffer washes isn't metaphorical corruption — it is quite literally money taken from a dead man's pocket.
And the spitting for luck is borrowed superstition — the river folk had rituals around the dead that stretched back centuries.
What's remarkable is that the novel never lets Gaffer's profession remain simply gothic — it keeps interrogating what money means and where moral worth actually lives.
Later, when we meet the Boffins — the Golden Dustman and his wife, people everyone dismisses as ignorant and unpolished — Dickens does something quietly extraordinary.
He gives us this almost polemical narrator's aside about the nature of goodness itself.
"For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never."
That is the novel's moral counter-argument to everything Gaffer represents.
Evil is finite, self-consuming; good propagates beyond itself.
Structurally, Dickens plants that idea early and spends the entire novel testing it.
And the test nearly breaks the novel, which is part of what makes it so gripping.
The Boffins are put through something quite dark before that maxim is vindicated — if it is vindicated.
But let's not get ahead of ourselves — we still have Gaffer to dispose of.
Which the river does, rather efficiently, as it turns out.
Gaffer's death is one of the novel's great dark ironies, and Dickens times it with almost brutal precision.
The man who made his living pulling the dead from the Thames ends up being pulled from it himself.
And the discovery is made by Riderhood — his own former partner, who had been hunting him.
Riderhood's reaction is just three words: 'Gaffer's done me. It's Gaffer!'
Not grief. Not even shock. Just the complaint of a man who has been cheated out of his revenge.
In three words Dickens tells you everything you need to know about Riderhood's moral universe.
'Done me' is extraordinary — it's the language of the marketplace applied to death.
Gaffer has somehow cheated Riderhood by dying — by removing himself from the economy of retribution.
It's a perfect callback to that opening scene where money is washed in river water — everything in this novel has a price, even a death.
The river gives and the river takes — and Dickens makes sure we feel both operations simultaneously.
We've established the world: dark, mercenary, the dead as currency.
In our next segment, we'll look more closely at identity itself — the novel's great game of who is pretending to be whom, and what Dickens makes of the whole charade.

segments.title: Money Made from Dust: Boffin's Moral Reckoning

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart — carefully, lovingly, and with a good deal of astonishment.
Today we're deep in the machinery of wealth: the Dust Heaps, the beggars who circle them, the blackmailers who think they've found a lever, and the moral cost of sudden money.
With me, as ever, are three brilliant guides to this extraordinary book.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing scholar who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a movement — always looking for the mechanism behind the effect.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what poverty looked like in Victorian England — and exactly what the law did and didn't do about it.
And Oliver Trevelyan has recorded more classic novels for audio than perhaps any living person — he hears the performance hidden in every Dickens sentence, and he brings it out.
We begin with the flood of letters that pours in on Boffin the Golden Dustman — charity appeals, schemes, petitions — and what Dickens does with them satirically.
What strikes me first about these charity-letter passages is the structural bravado of the thing.
Dickens doesn't give us one comic appeal — he gives us a taxonomy.
Fifty-seven churches, forty-two parsonage houses, seven-and-twenty organs — the accumulation is the joke, but it's also the argument.
He is showing us that notoriety functions like a magnet for every form of organized extraction.
And then, in the middle of all that comic cataloguing, he drops in the Duke of Linseed's letter — verbatim, mock-solemn, perfectly devastating.
The postscript is the masterpiece: 'The Steward's fee is limited to three Guineas.'
Limited. As if this is the duke's concession to Boffin's dignity.
The letter is even better than that, because Dickens tells us it was lithographed by the hundred — a mass-produced personal appeal.
The Duke hasn't written to Nicodemus Boffin at all — he's written to a slot where a wealthy man is supposed to fit.
What I love as a performer is the rhythm of that opening cry: 'Oh the varieties of dust for ocular use!'
'Oh the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold dust of the Golden Dustman!'
That exclamation belongs to the stage — it's a music-hall MC working a crowd, not a novelist quietly narrating.
Dickens knows the voice is doing the satirical work, and he gives it full throttle.
And the target is entirely real and entirely recognizable to Dickens's readers.

The Victorian charitable landscape was saturated with exactly this kind of aristocratic letterhead solicitation — where a duke lends his name, takes his cut of prestige, and the actual poor see almost nothing.
The Society for Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes — that name alone is a controlled explosion of class anxiety.
The middle classes are asking the newly wealthy to fund their own respectability — while a duke collects the organisational glory.
Which connects directly to the next passage — the individual beggars — where the satire gets darker and more uncomfortable.
Dickens gives the narrator this extraordinary simile for their letters, their so-called documents.
'They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf.'
That is a grotesquely specific image — and it's meant to sting, but it also captures something true about the gap between claim and reality.
The form of the document confers dignity; the content dissolves it.
The beggars on horseback section is where I think Dickens enjoys himself the most — the ones who have their spurs on, the steed is willing, but they simply require an astronomical telescope.
And then there are the beggars of punctual business-habits — my personal favourites — who will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday.
The precision of that deadline is so magnificent — it's desperation performing competence.
But I read the 'inspired beggars' quite differently — the ones sitting by a fragment of candle when an Angel whispered Boffin's name.
There's genuine cold and genuine darkness in that image — and Dickens lets it live alongside the comedy without resolving it.
That tension is historically accurate in the most uncomfortable way.
Begging letters were a genuine social phenomenon — and the recipients of them faced an impossible epistemic problem: which are fraudulent, which are real, and does it matter?
The daughters of general officers 'long accustomed to every luxury of life, except spelling' — that parenthesis is cruel, but it also does real social work.
It tells us that genteel poverty was partly about performance — and that performance was frequently unconvincing.
The comedy around money and class doesn't stop at letters and charity — it extends to how bodies look when money tries to dress them.
James, you were looking at the Sloppy passage — which is ostensibly about a suit of clothes, and is actually about rather more than that.
It is, and it repays close attention.

Rokesmith has given the tailor personal instructions to expend the utmost cunning of his art in concealing Sloppy's buttons — which immediately tells us the tailoring project is a kind of conspiracy against Sloppy's own body.
And the body wins, comprehensively.

Dickens's description is glorious: 'he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators.'
The Argus figure — the hundred-eyed giant of myth — is deployed here with perfect comic precision.
Sloppy cannot be made to look like he belongs to a world of polished respectability — his physical reality keeps erupting through the tailored surface.

The hatband is what finishes me — 'of wholesale capacity, which was fluted behind, from the crown of his hat to the brim, and terminated in a black bunch, from which the imagination shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted.'
The imagination shrunk discomfited! The reason revolted! These are philosophical faculties, entirely defeated by a hatband.
Dickens is doing something very specific: he applies the language of aesthetic judgement to an item of clothing that nobody in the scene would dare to criticise openly.
The comedy is entirely without cruelty toward Sloppy himself — the joke is on the hatter and the tailor and the system that produces this spectacle.
That's the craft move I want to underline — the narration refuses to make Sloppy the object of contempt.
The clothes are described as failing, the tailoring as defeated, the hatter's taste as incomprehensible — but Sloppy himself simply stands confessed, as Dickens puts it.
That phrase — 'Sloppy stood confessed' — is doing extraordinary double work.
It usually means revealed in one's true nature — here it means he is simply, undeniably, entirely himself, despite everything that has been done to reshape him.

From the comic irresistibility of Sloppy's buttons, we move to something considerably darker — the question of who else is watching the Boffin fortune, and what they plan to do with what they've found.
James, Wegg's scheme — and the earlier will he believes he's discovered — these are where the novel's satire on money turns genuinely sinister.
Wegg's reading of the earlier will is worth pausing on, because the document itself is a masterpiece of misanthropic legal terseness.

Wegg reads it out with visible satisfaction: 'Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown.'
'Quite enough for him' — that is a will that contains its own insult.
The testator is reaching from beyond the grave to deliver a final judgement on Boffin's worth — and then leaving everything else to an institution rather than a person.
Legally and psychologically, it is a document designed to humiliate as much as to dispose.
And Wegg's scheme, when he unfolds it, is structured with this grotesque parody of legal rigour — the 'conditional clause,' the 'comrade, brother, and partner' formula.
He's performing the language of business partnership to describe a blackmail conspiracy, and the gap between the register and the reality is where all the comedy and horror live.
The word he arrives at — 'Halves!' — is almost childlike in its simplicity after all the elaborate preamble.
Dickens sets it up so the punctuation itself delivers the punchline.
And then Wegg goes further — he's not satisfied with Halves, he muses whether it should be Two-thirds, or even Three-fourths.
'On those points he was ever open to correction.' That is the voice of a man who believes he is being scrupulously fair.
The phrase 'abject moral bondage and slavery' is what stays with me though — because it's not a comic phrase, even in Wegg's mouth.
The novel keeps finding these moments where the language of exploitation becomes suddenly literal and terrible — and you feel the full weight of what is being described.
That language recurs — in a much more concentrated and genuinely violent form — in the Riderhood and Headstone passage, which I find one of the most disturbing in the novel.
Riderhood has evidence — the Bargeman's clothes — and he knows exactly what evidence does in a power relationship.

His speech is relentless, hypnotic, and built around this triumphal repetition: 'I've got your Bargeman's clothes, tore this way and that way with the scuffle, stained green with the grass, and spattered all over with what bust from the blows.'
'I've got them, and I've got you.'
That is the grammar of possession — not of a thing, but of a person.
Wegg uses legal and commercial language to describe his hold on Boffin; Riderhood uses the language of physical evidence and physical dominance — and the effect is far colder.
The cadence of 'I'll be paid for it — I'll be paid for it — I'll be paid for it — till I've drained you dry' — that is prose written for the body, not just the mind.
The triple repetition with the dashes — Dickens is building a physical rhythm of obsession.
The phrase 'drained you dry' brings us back to liquids, to the river, to the extractive logic that runs through the whole novel.
The Dust Heaps, the begging letters, Wegg's schemes, Riderhood's blackmail — they're all versions of the same transaction: finding a source of wealth and draining it.
And Riderhood's boast — 'two could play at your game, and I played it long ago' — is the voice of someone who understands that every system of advantage has a counter-system waiting beneath it.
Bradley Headstone disguised himself to evade the social order — and Riderhood, who lives beneath that order, saw through the disguise immediately.
There's something almost grimly satisfying about it — and something entirely horrifying.

From ducal letterheads to blackmail, from a suit of buttons to a bundle of bloody clothes fished from the river — this novel keeps asking who profits and who pays, and the answers are rarely comfortable.
Thank you to Eleanor, James, and Oliver — and we'll be back shortly to follow the money further.

segments.title: A Gentleman in Disguise: The Architecture of Deceit

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We're deep inside one of the most elaborately constructed disguises in all of Victorian fiction.
John Harmon — heir to a dust-heap fortune — returns from abroad, survives an attempt on his life, and then slips quietly into his own inheritance as a secretary named John Rokesmith.
The question we're exploring today is: what does this architecture of deceit actually mean — morally, structurally, and in terms of sheer novelistic craft?
With me today are Eleanor Hartley, novelist and critic, who sees the skeleton beneath the prose — the structural choices that make a scene breathe.
James Blackstone, legal and social historian, who will tell us what all this inheritance business actually meant to a Victorian reader living under that law.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man whose voice has carried more Dickens to more ears than perhaps anyone living.
Oliver, let's start with you — because before we anatomise anything, someone needs to make the case for why this disguise plot works as storytelling.
The thing about Dickens is that he trusts his readers rather more than his readers trust him.
And he actually says so — in one of those gloriously unapologetic authorial asides he drops into the novel.
He tells us, quite plainly, that he was at great pains to suggest exactly what some readers assumed he was at great pains to conceal.

"I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he."
There's a magnificent cheek to that.
He's essentially saying: I knew you'd think you'd caught me out, and I'd already accounted for you.
The disguise plot isn't a mystery to be solved — it's a frame through which we watch a man rediscover who he is.
That reframing matters enormously.
Because if you read the Harmon disguise as a whodunit that fizzles, you'll be disappointed.
But if you read it as a structural device for withholding interiority — for keeping a man opaque to himself as much as to us — then it becomes something far more interesting.
Dickens gives Harmon a long, extraordinary interior monologue in which he literally tries to reconstruct who he is and what happened to him.
The disguise, then, isn't dishonesty — it's a holding pattern while identity reassembles itself.
And the Boffins are the moral anchor that makes that reassembly possible.
The Boffins — yes, let's go there, James.
Because old John Harmon — that monstrous patriarch — nonetheless puts these two people at the centre of his will.
What does that tell us, historically, about the kind of trust that wealth could or couldn't command?
The passage Dickens gives us about old Harmon and the Boffins is one of the sharpest things in the novel, and historians don't quote it nearly enough.
The narrator calls him 'the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail' — which tells you everything about how Dickens regards accumulated, isolated wealth.
But the crucial observation is this.
"he had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt"
The old man's one honest act — naming the Boffins in his will — stems not from affection but from frustrated avarice.
He couldn't corrupt them, so he had no choice but to trust them.
That is a precise and rather devastating account of how Victorian money actually operated in relation to moral character.
And what makes the Boffins so vivid — what Dickens earns — is that we see the cost before we see the reward.
Mr Boffin describes standing up for young John Harmon against the old man, again and again, until he ran out of names to call them.
And then he produces this extraordinary image — one of those moments where you realise Dickens is simultaneously being comic and devastating.

"I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet (she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head), and send it spinning across the yard."
The parenthetical — 'a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head' — is pure Dickens.
You see the bonnet, you see Mrs Boffin, you almost laugh — and then Boffin finishes his sentence.
'Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.'
The repetition is a full stop on your laughter.
That repetition is doing something very precise structurally.
Boffin is a man of limited verbal means — he doesn't have a sophisticated rhetorical arsenal.
So when the weight of what he's describing exceeds his language, he simply says the word again.
'Dropped her.' The first time is report. The second time is grief.
And it's in that gap — between a man's vocabulary and the enormity of his feeling — that Dickens locates so much of this novel's emotional truth.
It also tells us something about who gets to be eloquent about suffering in Victorian fiction — and who doesn't.
The educated, the propertied — they get the full sentence.
Boffin gets two words. But Dickens makes sure those two words hit harder than a paragraph.
The Boffins are, in a very real sense, the moral conscience of this novel — and they come from the dust.
Which makes Mrs Boffin's proposal about the orphan child all the more remarkable.
She inherits a vast fortune — and her first instinct is to find a child, name him John Harmon, and give the wealth meaning.
Eleanor — what does that gesture tell you about how Dickens uses the Boffins to interrogate inheritance itself?
It's one of the most quietly radical proposals in the book.
Mrs Boffin doesn't want to spend the money on status or comfort — she wants to use it to honour a memory and care for the living.
Listen to how she frames it — there's a beautiful tonal modulation Dickens gives her.
"Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him."
That cascade of 'and' — and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name and provide for him — is not clumsy syntax.
It's the rhythm of a woman thinking aloud, adding each act of care as it occurs to her.
It's tenderness rendered in grammatical form.
When you read that aloud — and I have, more times than I can count — the polysyndeton does something an actor almost can't improve on.
Each 'and' is a small act of will. You feel the generosity accumulating.
She ends with 'Say it's only a whim' — which is her way of pre-empting anyone who might call her sentimental.
But of course it isn't a whim. It's a theology.
And then we arrive at the scene where Harmon — now unmasked — faces Silas Wegg.
Harmon makes an extraordinary declaration about the source of his fortune — one that formally repudiates the logic of inheritance by birth.
"I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin."
The parenthesis — 'there are no words to satisfy me' — is as significant as anything else in that sentence.
Harmon arrives at the limits of language precisely when speaking of virtue — just as Boffin did when speaking of Mrs Boffin being dropped.
The novel keeps insisting that genuine goodness exceeds what formal language can hold.
James, that connection is brilliant — I hadn't placed those two parenthetical failures of language side by side before.
And it vindicates Oliver's point about the disguise plot being about identity rather than mystery.
Harmon spends the whole novel watching the Boffins to see if they are what they appear to be.
And when he finally speaks openly about them, language fails — which is Dickens's way of marking something as genuinely beyond price.
That's a remarkable throughline — the inadequacy of language as a marker of authentic moral value.
And it cuts right against the novel's many characters who are very fluent indeed about their own virtue — none of them trustworthy.
We'll be taking up the question of trust and its counterfeits — and the world those counterfeits inhabit — in our next segment.
Stay with us.

segments.title: Bella's Appetite: Gold, Love, and the Woman Unmasked

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
Today we're going deep on one of the novel's most compelling questions: what does Bella Wilfer actually want, and what does Dickens do to her in order to find out?
To help us think through that, we have three guests whose perspectives couldn't be better suited to this material.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — always for the hidden gears.
Professor James Blackstone brings the social and legal history — the real texture of what money, class, and charity meant in Victorian England.
And Oliver Trevelyan, actor, writer, and the man who has read more Dickens aloud than perhaps anyone living, is here to make sure we hear the prose as performance.
Let's begin with the world Bella inhabits — a world where social identity is as fungible as furniture.
What strikes me first, every time I return to this novel, is how Dickens frames social performance before we've even met the main characters.
The Twemlow passage is almost absurdly economical — he turns a human being into furniture in a single sentence.
And then he extends the conceit with complete architectural seriousness.
Listen to how it works:
"Being first cousin to Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state."
The word 'represent' is doing enormous work there.
Twemlow doesn't merely attend dinners — he constitutes them, socially speaking, by virtue of a family connection he didn't earn and cannot really use.
And when the table is pulled out to its full twenty leaves, poor Twemlow finds himself furthest from the center — that's the satirical sting embedded in the metaphor.
And that's not merely comic invention — it reflects a perfectly real social mechanism.
The Veneerings are new money — their very name tells you that — and they need what Twemlow's cousinship with Lord Snigsworth confers: the appearance of legitimacy.
What Dickens captures so precisely is that the Veneerings don't actually need Twemlow to do anything — they need him to be present.
His function is purely symbolic, which is why the furniture metaphor is so accurate and so devastating.
It's the same logic that governs Boffin's charity books, later in the novel.
The title matters more than the substance — whether you're a Patron or a Patroness, a Vice-Patron or an Ex-Vice-Patroness.
The charity catalogue is one of the great comic set-pieces in the whole novel, and Boffin delivers it with exactly the right degree of baffled outrage.
When I read it aloud, the trick is to let the list build its own momentum — you can hear Dickens timing the joke with absolute precision.
Boffin says:

"Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!"
'Pretty well up to his neck' — that's the landing.
The list is comic in its accretion, but that final image of Rokesmith physically drowning in paperwork earns a genuine laugh every time.
And crucially, it reveals Boffin's moral clarity — he sees through the pretension instantly, even if he can't always articulate why it bothers him.
That moral clarity in Boffin is interesting precisely because it works as a foil for Bella's arc.
Bella at this stage of the novel has an appetite for money that she's almost refreshingly honest about.
She's not a hypocrite in the mode of the Veneerings — she doesn't pretend her ambitions are something finer.
What Dickens is doing structurally is placing her in this environment of gilded pretension and then asking: can desire be educated?
And the answer comes partly through her exposure to genuine suffering — the kind Lizzie describes with such devastating plainness.
The passage about the child and the drunken household — that's Dickens at his most directly polemical, and it earns it.
Lizzie is describing a world that Dickens's first readers would have recognized with uncomfortable immediacy.
Drink was genuinely catastrophic in the riverside parishes — the statistics from the 1860s are staggering.
But what I find remarkable is the line's precision.
Lizzie says:
"This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley."
That parenthetical — 'if she ever had one' — is quietly devastating.
It acknowledges, without sentimentality, that the very material preconditions of childhood — a cradle, a safe beginning — are not guaranteed.
It's the most quietly placed horror in the sentence, and Lizzie delivers it almost as an afterthought — which is exactly what makes it land.
Dickens knew that understatement in the midst of plain speech hits harder than rhetoric.
And there's a counterpoint here to Charley — who by this point in the novel has become rather a disagreeable study in self-advancement.
Charley's indictment of Bradley Headstone is all the more withering because it's entirely self-referential.
He accuses Bradley of selfishness in terms that perfectly describe his own moral condition.
He tells Headstone:
"you are in all your passions so selfish, and so concentrated upon yourself that you have not bestowed one proper thought on me."
'One proper thought on me' — the accusation of selfishness ends in pure self-pity, and Dickens leaves that irony completely unglossed.
That unglossed irony is one of Dickens's most sophisticated tools in this novel.
He trusts the reader completely — he doesn't nudge you toward the correct response.
And that connects to the extraordinary train passage — which is doing something structurally very bold.
The novel suddenly pulls back to this vast, impersonal perspective — the train as a great rocket, indifferent to all human turnings.
The passage ends:

"the train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded in the rush of smoke and steam and glare."
That image — the bomb-shell bursting over the quiet river — is doing moral and metaphysical work simultaneously.
The river is always patience, mystery, continuity in this novel — and the train violates it with contemptuous force, and then it's simply gone.
The railway in the 1860s was still genuinely felt as a violent intrusion — whole neighborhoods demolished for the lines, as the passage records with those 'ragged sides of houses torn down.'
Dickens is not being sentimental about a lost pastoral — he's registering the actual texture of destruction.
And the comparison to Father Time — 'going straight to its end, as Father Time goes to his' — that's genuinely ominous in the context of the plot at this moment.
And the ominousness crystallizes in the Bradley passage — which is perhaps the most formally strange piece of sustained prose in the novel.
It reads almost like stage directions for a Gothic performance — the rigidity, the fire, the slow visible deterioration.
Dickens writes:

"Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes."
'Charmed flame turning him old' — he's not just aging, he's being consumed by his own obsession, and Dickens renders it as a kind of terrible enchantment.
It's the moral logic of the whole novel compressed into a single visual image.
What I find striking is how all of these images — the furniture-man, the drowning secretary, the bomb-shell train, the man turning to ash — form a kind of grammar of value in the novel.
Things that should be human are made into objects, and objects are given terrifying agency.
Bella's story is about whether she can reverse that logic — whether she can resist the world's pressure to treat herself as a commodity.
We'll continue that question in our next segment, looking at the river itself — the novel's great silent protagonist.

segments.title: Dustmen, Dust-Contractors, and the Machinery of Greed

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously as the great, strange, magnificent thing it is.
Today we're deep in the world of dust mounds, deception, and disguise — and the comic machinery that drives so much of this novel's plot.
With me today: Dr Eleanor Hartley, novelist and creative writing scholar, who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — with absolute delight in how it all fits.
Prof James Blackstone, legal and social historian, whose knowledge of Victorian institutions makes the novel's satire land with doubled force.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man whose voice has brought more Dickens to life than perhaps anyone living.
Oliver, I want to start with you, because this segment belongs to the comic genius of this novel — and you have a feel for that like no one else.
We have Eugene Wrayburn, who is one of the great idlers in all of English fiction, and you've been sitting with a passage where he defines himself in the most magnificently useless terms imaginable.
Eugene Wrayburn is a man who has elevated purposelessness into an art form, and I mean that as the highest compliment.
He is one of those characters who exists almost entirely as a performance — performed for Mortimer, for himself, for the novel's reader.
And in this moment with Mortimer, Dickens gives him a speech of extraordinary self-description.

"You know how dreadfully susceptible I am to boredom. You know that when I became enough of a man to find myself an embodied conundrum, I bored myself to the last degree by trying to find out what I meant."
An embodied conundrum. That's the phrase. He tried to solve himself and found it too dull to continue.
And then he quotes — or rather misquotes, charmingly — a children's nursery riddle.
His reply being, 'No. Upon my life, I can't.' Which is, I think, both comic and genuinely poignant at once.
What strikes me about that speech is the structural cleverness — Dickens has Eugene doing something very precise there.
He turns self-ignorance into a rhetorical performance of self-knowledge. The man who claims he cannot know himself speaks with absolute fluency about the contours of that unknowing.
It's a form of irony that implicates Eugene himself — he's far more self-aware than he's willing to admit, and the speech exposes that.
The nursery riddle at the end is a masterpiece of tonal management — it deflates before the sentiment can solidify into anything earnest.
Dickens uses Eugene to do that constantly — sensation is allowed to surface, then lightly mocked, then set aside.

I'd add that Eugene's ennui is historically very specific. He is a barrister with no practice, a gentleman with no function, a product of a system that trained men for a world that had no particular use for them.

The boredom isn't personal weakness — it's structural. The law as an institution, in Dickens's rendering, is a machine that grinds without producing anything of value for most of the people inside it.
And the phrase 'embodied conundrum' quietly describes the whole class of idle professional men that Victorian society produced in abundance and then had nowhere to put.
James, that's the thing — Dickens is laughing, but he's laughing at something that genuinely pains him.
Now — can we move to a very different kind of comedy, because Mrs Sprodgkin deserves her moment.
This passage with the Milveys is a small gem of satirical writing that I think gets undervalued.
Mrs Sprodgkin is described as possessing, and I love this, a sixth sense for knowing when the Reverend Frank Milvey least desired her company.
"she regarded tea and sugar in the light of myrrh and frankincense, and considered bread and butter identical with locusts and wild honey."
The audacity of that comparison. She accepts the bribe and then reframes it as religious scripture. It's a complete theological rebranding of a pat of butter.
And yet Dickens doesn't let the satire crush the Milveys — that's the careful thing.
They hurry to the railway station in a heated condition, which is undignified and human and endearing.
And then comes that authorial aside — about how they 'merge the smallness of their work in its greatness' and feel no danger of losing dignity when they accommodate incomprehensible humbugs.
That is Dickens writing as a moralist — but doing it so quickly and so wryly that you almost miss it.
Good people are funny and sweating and hurried, and that doesn't diminish them. It's a quietly radical idea about goodness.

Mrs Sprodgkin is also a very accurate portrait of what the parish clergy actually had to manage — a class of parishioner who treated the church as a source of material relief and theatrical grievance in equal measure.
The question about 'who begat whom' and the Amorites — these are not invented absurdities. Dickens knew exactly the kind of querulous Biblical pedantry that drove overworked clergy mad.
The welfare implications are real too — buying someone off with tea, bread, and butter describes the actual informal economy of Victorian parish charity. Bread and butter was not nothing.
Right — and now we come to one of my favourite revelations in the whole novel, because it involves Sloppy, and Sloppy is a gift.
Wegg has been plagued by this menacing figure — the ever-wakeful dustman — and now the disguise falls away.
Dickens writes it in one single, beautifully constructed sentence. Here it is:
"Somebody else had come in quietly by the folding-doors. Turning his head, Wegg beheld his persecutor, the ever-wakeful dustman, accoutred with fantail hat and velveteen smalls complete.
Who, untying his tied-up broken head, revealed a head that was whole, and a face that was Sloppy's."
'A face that was Sloppy's.' That's the whole trick — all that menace, all that velveteen authority, and it's been Sloppy all along.
It's the comedy of the innocent as agent of justice, which is one of Dickens's deepest pleasures.
The syntax of that sentence does everything — 'Who, untying his tied-up broken head, revealed a head that was whole.' That relative clause is doing the work of a conjuror's reveal.
Dickens delays the name 'Sloppy' to the absolute last word. It's the punchline position. He knows exactly what he's doing.
And 'fantail hat and velveteen smalls complete' — that catalog of costume is so specific it's almost affectionate. Even Wegg's tormentor gets a wardrobe.
The fantail hat and velveteen smalls were the genuine working uniform of the dustman trade in Victorian London — Dickens is being documentary here as well as comic.

The dustman as a figure carried enormous symbolic weight — these were the men who sorted through the fortunes of the dead, working in the shadow of the great dust mounds that generated the Boffin inheritance.

Sloppy wearing that costume to unmask Wegg is a kind of rough justice that has its roots in the actual culture of the trade — a recognition that the dust mounds belong to those who worked them, not those who tried to steal them.
And then — before we leave the comedy entirely — there's Bella's scene with Mr Boffin, which moves the needle from comic to genuinely tender in about four sentences.
She puts the baby in John's arms, she kneels beside Boffin, and she speaks.
And the register of that speech is extraordinary — it's childlike, but not childish.
"Please I have found out something not yet mentioned. Please I don't believe you are a hard-hearted miser at all, and please I don't believe you ever for one single minute were!"
The repetition of 'please' — it's like a child's grammar of appeal, but what's being said is a full moral reversal of everything that came before.
Dickens uses the simplest possible syntax to carry the heaviest possible emotional freight. That's mastery.
The baby is doing structural work in that scene as well — Bella places the Inexhaustible, as Dickens calls the child, in John's arms before she kneels.
It's a staging choice. She frees her hands, she lowers herself physically, she gives herself over to the gesture completely.
And Boffin 'had moved to a table where he was leaning his head upon his hand with his face turned away' — he cannot bear to receive it directly.
The comedy of forcing him to turn his 'delighted face' — with that exultant ringing laugh — is Dickens allowing joy to be physical and undignified and completely real.
What I hear in all of these passages is Dickens using comedy as a carrier wave for something much more serious — identity, justice, moral transformation.
The laughter never cancels the weight — it somehow makes it bearable to feel.
We'll return after the break to look more closely at the language of greed and how Dickens builds his villains — and his redeemable near-villains — through the texture of their speech.

segments.title: The Comic Masks: Wit and Folly in the World of Wealth

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — and joyfully.
I'm your host, and today we're examining a passage that sits at the very moral and psychological heart of the novel.
John Harmon's long, solitary reckoning with himself — his inheritance, his disguise, his father's corrupting legacy — and what it means to test the woman he's supposed to marry.
To help us unpack all of this, I'm delighted to have three quite remarkable readers with me.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing scholar who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — for the engineering behind the magic.
Professor James Blackstone brings legal and social history — he can tell us what these institutions actually were, what the money actually meant, and why it mattered.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic novels than anyone alive — who hears every Dickens sentence as a piece of music written for performance.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — because what strikes me immediately about these chapters is the peculiar structure of John Harmon's confession.
He's not speaking to anyone, really — he's reasoning with himself, almost forensically.
Yes, and that forensic quality is precisely the point — Dickens is doing something formally extraordinary here.
John Harmon talks to himself in the second person — 'Now, stop, and so far think it out, John Harmon.'
'Is that so? That is exactly so.'
He's prosecuting himself — and then acquitting himself — within the same breath.
What Dickens has built is essentially an interior courtroom, with Harmon as both witness and judge.
And the repetition — 'I have all these facts right? Yes. They are all accurately right' — performs the act of self-interrogation as ritual.
It's Dickens showing us a man who has been so defined by mistrust that he can only trust himself by cross-examining himself.
And the source of that mistrust is devastatingly specific — it isn't abstract psychological damage, it's the money.
Dickens understood, with almost sociological precision, how inherited wealth distorts every relationship it touches.
Consider what Harmon actually says when he arrives back in England — the passage is worth sitting with.
'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife.'
That triple rhythm — shrinking, shrinking, mistrustful — is not ornamental.
He is already contaminated by what he's supposedly fled.
The fortune produces its corruption before he's even touched a penny of it — that's the mechanism Dickens is exposing.
And the test he devises for Bella — dressing as a common sailor, watching her without her knowledge — is itself a product of that corruption.
James is right to call it corruption — but I want to linger on just how darkly comic the sailor scheme actually is.
Here is a man of considerable fortune, and the plan he arrives at — with a near-stranger on a boat — is to put on a sailor's costume and lurk around a girl's neighbourhood.
Dickens gives us the method with such deadpan specificity:
'the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way.'
And then — 'doing whatever chance might favour on the spot.'
Whatever chance might favour on the spot — this is his plan.
The man has been agonising over this inheritance for years, and his operational strategy is essentially — improvise.
And yet the comedy doesn't undercut the tragedy — it intensifies it.
By the time we reach the chapter thirty-one retrospective, Dickens is tracing how this improvised deception hardened into something Harmon could no longer control.
The narrator's framing is almost clinical in its precision:
'he had lapsed into the condition in which he found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances.'
'Accumulative power' — that phrase is doing an enormous amount of work.
It mirrors the novel's central metaphor — the way wealth itself accumulates, passively, lethally, without any individual act of malice.
And the legal trap Harmon finds himself in is genuinely impossible — Dickens has constructed it with real precision.
By coming back to life and accepting the inheritance, he must buy Bella — his word, essentially.
By coming back to life and rejecting it, he punishes her — deprives her of the fortune she'd been promised.
Dickens articulates this dilemma with almost forensic cruelty:
'Was it for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?'
This is the Victorian marriage market laid perfectly bare — there is no honourable exit from a system built on the commodification of women.
What makes it bearable to perform — and I have read this aloud — is that Dickens never lets Harmon become merely a victim of circumstance.
He did choose this.
And Dickens gives us the exact moment of that choice — lying in a sick bed above a public-house, feverish and half-drowned.
'the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella.'
'Proving Bella' — two words that contain the whole novel's moral problem.
Can you prove a person?
And if you must put someone through a test to trust them — what does that say about your capacity for love?
That's the question Dickens refuses to answer tidily.
The deception was 'meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days' — that's Harmon's self-justification.
'When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood... he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless.'
'Meant to be harmless' is not the same as harmless — and the novel knows it, even if Harmon doesn't quite.
The architecture here is almost novelistic in the strict sense — Dickens has layered three temporal perspectives simultaneously.
There's what Harmon intended, what actually happened, and what the narrator now sees with retrospective clarity.
What a nest of contradictions Dickens has built here — a man trying to escape his father's corruption by enacting a corruption of his own.
Oliver, before we move on — as a performer, when you read these passages aloud, is there a single moment that lands differently than it reads on the page?
Always the same moment, without fail.
It's the final self-correction in the chapter thirty passage — after the long catalogue of mistrust and shrinking and fear.
He lists everything that drove him back to England and then simply asks himself:
'Now, stop, and so far think it out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.'
On the page it reads as self-interrogation.
But read aloud, with any kind of silence before 'That is exactly so' — it becomes grief.
A man confirming to himself, alone, in the dark, the full weight of his own wretchedness.
That's a remarkable place to pause — and a perfect note on which to carry this conversation forward.
We've seen how Dickens uses John Harmon's confession to expose the machinery of inherited wealth — its distortions, its traps, its slow corruptions.
In our next segment, we'll turn outward — to the social world that wealth constructs around these characters, and the masks it demands they wear.

segments.title: Our Mutual Friend: Inheritance, Identity, and the Redemption of Gold

utterances.text: We've ranged across a great deal of territory today — the dust mounds, the river, the drawing rooms of the nouveaux riches.
But I want to close where the novel's heart really beats — in moments of tenderness, memory, and what it might mean to be redeemed.

Eleanor, I wonder if we could begin with Boffin — because there's a passage in which he recalls young John Harmon as a child of seven, and it's one of the most quietly devastating things in the whole novel.
It really is devastating — and what's remarkable is that Dickens gives it to Boffin to tell, in Boffin's own voice, which is not a literary voice at all.
Boffin speaks in the dialect of the yard, the dust-heap, the working life.
And yet through that voice comes something almost unbearable in its simplicity.
Dickens sets it up so carefully — the little scanty travelling clothes, the little scanty box, the shivering wind.
"There was his little scanty travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the steamboat."
That repetition of 'little scanty' — it's not elegant writing by conventional standards, but it's perfect writing.
Each word is a small blow, and the accumulation is merciless.
And that's where the performance lives, isn't it — in the repetition, the rhythm of the thing.
When I read Boffin aloud, I have to resist the temptation to smooth him out, to make him more 'correct.'
His roughness is precisely the point.
And then you get to Mrs Boffin's cry — and it just opens up entirely.
"She holds him round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, 'I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!'"
'The wide wide world' — that reduplication is pure spoken English, not written English.
Dickens is transcribing the sound of a heart breaking — not describing it, transcribing it.
What strikes me — and I think this is worth holding onto — is the institutional cruelty operating just beneath that tenderness.
'The old man wouldn't hear of allowing a sixpence coach-money.' That single detail tells you everything about old Harmon's regime.
A child of seven is being sent abroad, alone, and his father will not pay sixpence to spare him the cold walk to the dock.
And the fortune — the monstrous fortune in dust — is sitting there accumulating.
That is the novel's great indictment: wealth does not prevent cruelty.
In many cases in this book, wealth generates it.
And that's precisely why the novel needs its counter-images — spaces where something like grace operates outside the money economy.
There's that extraordinary scene on the rooftop — Riah's rooftop garden — with Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren.
Dickens gives them a carpet spread among the chimney-stacks, books, fruit, strings of beads.
"Seated on it, against no more romantic object than a blackened chimney-stack over which some bumble creeper had been trained, they both pored over one book; both with attentive faces."
That phrase — 'no more romantic object than a blackened chimney-stack' — is doing something very precise.
It's claiming the right to find beauty in the industrial and the urban — and then delivering it, quietly, without fanfare.
And the surrounding chimneys — bridling and fanning themselves and looking on in 'a state of airy surprise.'
That's Dickens in his element — the comic grotesque suddenly made tender.
The industrial cityscape becomes a crowd of baffled onlookers who don't quite know what to make of these two women reading.
And what they're reading matters — they're educating themselves, in secret, on a rooftop, with no patron and no permission.
That is a quietly radical act in Dickens's world.
The rooftop is also, I think, an explicitly utopian space — it is above the city, outside ordinary commerce and surveillance.

Riah provides it — and the gentle Jew is a figure Dickens uses partly in conscious reparation for Fagin, partly as a genuine embodiment of a kind of mercy that the Christian mercantile world has entirely abandoned.
It is worth noting that what Riah offers is precisely what the novel celebrates: small, material acts of care that money can enable but never replace.
A carpet, a basket of fruit, a few books.
And that's the key to how the novel ends its emotional argument, isn't it — through the smallest possible things.
There's a dinner scene with Bella and John Rokesmith and old Wilfer — and it's just supper in an office, essentially.
But Dickens describes it like this — and I want to read it because you simply cannot paraphrase it:

"It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, 'Somebody's been drinking my milk!'"
"It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made."
The joy in that sentence is infectious — and Dickens earns it.
These people have come through real loss to sit in a counting-house eating a modest supper and calling it the finest meal of their lives.
What I love about that passage is the iron safe in the corner — the eyes of a 'dull dragon.'
The money-world is still present, still watching — Chicksey, Veneering, and Stobbles — but it's been reduced to a comic background detail.
The dragon has been tamed not by defeating it but by simply not caring about it for an evening.
That, I think, is Dickens's most mature statement about wealth: you cannot abolish it, but you can, on occasion, render it irrelevant.
I'll admit that gives me a certain unease — politically speaking.
Because the dragon is still there.
Riderhood still accuses Gaffer Hexam with the certainty of a man who knows the law will listen to him.
'The hand of Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the hand that done that deed. His hand and no other.'
That rhythm — 'his hand and no other' — it's the rhythm of a sworn deposition, of institutional power being mobilized.
And the novel knows that all its pastoral rooftops and hobgoblin suppers exist alongside that world — not in place of it.
That's exactly right — and it's why the novel doesn't feel sentimental, even in its most tender moments.
Dickens is always aware of the cold outside — the shivering wind around that little box.
Joy, in this novel, is real — but it is hard won, and it is provisional.
Which is perhaps the most honest thing any novel can offer us — joy that knows what it costs.
Our Mutual Friend has been our companion today — and what a companion it is: funny, grieving, politically awake, and shot through with moments of extraordinary grace.
My warmest thanks to Eleanor Hartley, James Blackstone, and Oliver Trevelyan — three readers of unusual intelligence and genuine feeling.
And to you listening: if you haven't read this novel, please do — and if you have, perhaps today has given you reason to return to it.
This has been Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.

c9:p29.text:
These two ignorant and unpolished people had guided themselves so far on
      in their journey of life, by a religious sense of duty and desire to do
      right. Ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities might have been detected in
      the breasts of both; ten thousand vanities additional, possibly, in the
      breast of the woman. But the hard wrathful and sordid nature that had
      wrung as much work out of them as could be got in their best days, for as
      little money as could be paid to hurry on their worst, had never been so
      warped but that it knew their moral straightness and respected it. In its
      own despite, in a constant conflict with itself and them, it had done so.
      And this is the eternal law. For, Evil often stops short at itself and
      dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.
c9:p29.summary: Dickens reflects that the Boffins, though ignorant and unpolished, have been guided by genuine religious duty and moral righteousness that even hardened souls cannot entirely resist.
c9:p29.best_quote: For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

c27:p51.text:
The consideration of Mrs Boffin had clothed Mr Sloppy in a suit of black,
      on which the tailor had received personal directions from Rokesmith to
      expend the utmost cunning of his art, with a view to the concealment of
      the cohering and sustaining buttons. But, so much more powerful were the

On this head, Silas Wegg had much to say. Silas had to say That, he would
      beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner, of the impressive
      passages they had read that evening; of the evident parallel in Mr
      Boffin’s mind between them and the late owner of the Bower, and the
      present circumstances of the Bower; of the bottle; and of the box. That,
      the fortunes of his brother and comrade, and of himself were evidently
      made, inasmuch as they had but to put their price upon this document, and
      get that price from the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour: who
      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’
      That, the question then arose when ‘Halves!’ should be called. That, here
      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.
      It was not to be borne that the minion and worm should carry off any of
      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points
      he was ever open to correction.

      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to

      while it was his daily declaration that he mistrusted all mankind—and

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.

c8:p43.text:
‘The last time me and Mrs Boffin saw the poor boy,’ said Mr Boffin,
      warming (as fat usually does) with a tendency to melt, ‘he was a child of
      seven year old. For when he came back to make intercession for his sister,
      me and Mrs Boffin were away overlooking a country contract which was to be
      sifted before carted, and he was come and gone in a single hour. I say he
      was a child of seven year old. He was going away, all alone and forlorn,
      to that foreign school, and he come into our place, situate up the yard of
      the present Bower, to have a warm at our fire. There was his little scanty
      travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in
      the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the
      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God
      bless you!” and for a moment rests his heart against her bosom, and looks
      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),
      and I left him when he had fallen asleep in his berth, and I came back to
      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was
      very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would
      wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, “Don’t you see the poor child’s
      face? O shelter the poor child!”—till in course of years it gently
      wore out, as many things do.’
c8:p43.summary: Boffin recounts the last time he and Mrs Boffin saw young John Harmon, a seven-year-old being sent to a foreign school, including the poignant moment when Mrs Boffin wept while warming the boy by the fire and embraced him protectively, expressing a desire to save him—a memory that haunted her for years.

Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren. For whom, perhaps with some old instinct of
      his race, the gentle Jew had spread a carpet. Seated on it, against no
      more romantic object than a blackened chimney-stack over which some bumble
      creeper had been trained, they both pored over one book; both with
      attentive faces; Jenny with the sharper; Lizzie with the more perplexed.
      Another little book or two were lying near, and a common basket of common
      fruit, and another basket full of strings of beads and tinsel scraps. A
      few boxes of humble flowers and evergreens completed the garden; and the
      encompassing wilderness of dowager old chimneys twirled their cowls and
      fluttered their smoke, rather as if they were bridling, and fanning
      themselves, and looking on in a state of airy surprise.

It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three
      nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous
      low growlings of the alarming discovery, ‘Somebody’s been drinking  my 
      milk!’ It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or

c12:p93.text:
‘Now let me be took down again,’ said Riderhood, when he had turned the
      drowned cap over and under, and had brushed it the wrong way (if it had a
      right way) with his sleeve. ‘I give information that the man that done the
      Harmon Murder is Gaffer Hexam, the man that found the body. The hand of
      Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the
      hand that done that deed. His hand and no other.’
